title: 22. Interview: Global Load Balancing
summary: Interview Q&A for Global Load Balancing — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Global Load Balancing interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between global load balancing and regular (local) load balancing?
**Answer:** A regular load balancer distributes traffic across servers in a single data center or availability zone — it operates at the L4/L7 level, sees one pool of backends, and picks based on RR/LC/health. A global load balancer distributes traffic across multiple geographic regions (data centers in different cities, often different continents), operating primarily at the DNS layer or via anycast. The key difference is the routing criterion: local LB cares about server load and connection state; global LB cares about geography (latency, distance), regional health, and capacity weights. Local LB sees the client only as a TCP source IP; global LB sees the client's country or /24 prefix and chooses a region accordingly. Local LB failover is sub-second (TCP re-establish); global LB failover is bounded by DNS TTL (typically 60 seconds). Real-world: a single AWS ALB is local LB; Route 53 latency-based routing across multiple ALBs in different regions is global LB.
**Visual:**
```
Local LB:                        Global LB:
client -> ALB -> [B1,B2,B3]     client -> DNS -> region -> ALB -> [B1..Bn]
        (one region)                  (multiple regions)
        failover: ms                  failover: ~TTL seconds
```

### Q2. How does latency-based DNS routing work, and what is EDNS Client Subnet?
**Answer:** Latency-based routing returns the region IP with the lowest measured network latency to the user. To know "lowest latency to this user," the authoritative nameserver needs to know roughly where the user is — but a recursive DNS resolver (like 8.8.8.8) hides the user's IP. EDNS Client Subnet (ECS) is an extension where the resolver includes the user's /24 prefix in the DNS query, so the authoritative nameserver knows the user's network location. The DNS provider (Route 53, Cloudflare, NS1) operates a global probing network that continuously measures latency from each /24 to each region, then returns the closest region's IP. Without ECS, the nameserver falls back to the resolver's IP, which can be wildly inaccurate (e.g., a user in Tokyo using Google's 8.8.8.8 resolver in the US would be routed to the US region). Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 disables ECS by default for privacy, falling back to its own PoP location, which works well for anycast CDNs but less well for origin latency routing.
**Visual:**
```
User(203.0.113.5) -> resolver -> authoritative DNS
                                  query carries ECS: 203.0.113.0/24
                                  DNS: latency map says APAC=8ms -> return APAC IP
                                  (without ECS: only sees resolver IP -> wrong region)
```

### Q3. What is anycast and why doesn't it work for long-lived TCP connections?
**Answer:** Anycast means the same IP address is announced from multiple locations via BGP. The Internet's routing infrastructure delivers each packet to the nearest announcement (by BGP shortest-path), so a user in Tokyo hitting anycast IP `1.1.1.1` reaches Cloudflare's Tokyo PoP while a user in Berlin reaches Frankfurt. Anycast is elegant: zero DNS cleverness required, latency is automatically minimized, and DDoS attacks are diluted across all announcement sites. The limitation is that BGP routes can change mid-connection — if a route flaps, packets in an existing TCP flow can suddenly start arriving at a different PoP that has no context for the connection, breaking it. So anycast works for short or connectionless protocols (DNS over UDP, NTP, HTTP/3 over QUIC) but not for long-lived TCP. CDNs work around this by terminating TCP at the edge PoP (the connection's "near end") and re-originating a separate unicast TCP back to the origin, so the anycast hop is only the client-to-edge leg.
**Visual:**
```
anycast: 1.1.1.1 announced from 300 PoPs
   Tokyo user -----> Tokyo PoP     (BGP nearest)
   Berlin user -----> Frankfurt PoP (BGP nearest)

risk: BGP route change mid-connection
   Tokyo user ====TCP==== Tokyo PoP   ...route flaps...
   Tokyo user ====TCP==== Seattle PoP  (no TCP state!) -> connection breaks
```

### Q4. Compare active-active vs active-passive multi-region architectures.
**Answer:** Active-active serves live traffic from all regions simultaneously, with each region running at full capacity and capable of serving all users. Traffic is split by latency/geo/weight. Failover is fast: when a region dies, DNS health checks stop returning its IP, and within the TTL window (~60s) all clients re-resolve to the next-best region. Cost is high — you pay for full capacity in every region, and you must replicate data across regions (DynamoDB Global Tables, Spanner). Netflix uses active-active across three AWS regions. Active-passive keeps one region hot (serving traffic) and others warm (scaled down to minimum capacity). On failure of the primary, you scale up the backup and shift DNS. Failover is slow (minutes to scale up) but cost is low (you pay for one full region + minimal warm capacity). The choice depends on RTO (recovery time objective): active-active targets seconds-to-minutes; active-passive targets minutes-to-tens-of-minutes. Most enterprises start active-passive for cost reasons and migrate to active-active as they grow.
**Visual:**
```
active-active:        active-passive:
  EU <--> US <--> APAC    EU (hot)  US (warm, idle)  APAC (warm, idle)
  all serve traffic       EU fails -> scale US up -> DNS shift (5-15 min)
  failover: 60s (DNS TTL)
```

### Q5. Why is DNS TTL a critical parameter in global load balancing, and what are the trade-offs?
**Answer:** DNS TTL controls how long a client or resolver may cache a DNS response before re-querying. In global LB, TTL is the upper bound on failover time: if a region fails, clients with cached IPs continue hitting the dead region until the TTL expires and they re-resolve. A long TTL (1 hour) reduces DNS query load and lets clients cache aggressively, but failover takes up to 1 hour — unacceptable for an SLA. A short TTL (60s) enables ~60-second failover but increases DNS query volume (every client re-resolves every minute), making the DNS provider a hot path and a single point of failure. Route 53 recommends 60s for active-active multi-region. Some providers (Cloudflare) use 5-minute TTLs with aggressive pre-fetching by resolvers, balancing load and failover. The DNS provider itself must be highly available (anycast DNS, multiple authoritative nameservers) — if DNS is down, even a perfectly healthy origin is unreachable. A common production pattern is 60s TTL during steady state, lowered to 10s during a known incident window for faster re-routing.
**Visual:**
```
TTL=3600s (1h):  1 DNS query/hour, failover up to 1 hour
TTL=60s:         60 queries/hour, failover in 60 seconds  <-- typical
TTL=10s:         360 queries/hour, failover in 10 seconds (incident mode)
```

### Q6. How does multi-region data replication interact with global load balancing?
**Answer:** Global LB routes the user to the closest region, but if the user's data lives in only one region, the request must cross-continent to fetch it — defeating the latency benefit. So active-active global LB requires multi-region data replication: writes are propagated to all regions so any region can serve any user's reads. Two consistency models exist: **eventual consistency** (DynamoDB Global Tables, Cassandra) — writes return after local ack, propagate to other regions in under a second, but a write in EU may not yet be visible in US during that window — acceptable for most user-facing apps (watchlists, profile settings). **Strong consistency** (Spanner, CockroachDB) — writes synchronously replicate across regions, guaranteeing linearizability, but each write pays cross-region RTT (50-150ms) — only justified for financial transactions. The architecture choice cascades: read-heavy workloads with eventual consistency (DynamoDB) are the common pattern for global consumer apps; strong consistency (Spanner) is reserved for low-write-rate critical-state services. Conflict resolution (last-write-wins, application-level merge) is the operational cost of eventual consistency.
**Visual:**
```
EU write -> DynamoDB Global Table -> propagates to US, APAC in <1s
                                     (eventual consistency)
user in US reads watchlist -> served from US replica (eventually consistent)
```

### Q7. What are the layers of health checking needed for reliable global load balancing?
**Answer:** A single-layer health check is insufficient. You need three. (1) **DNS-layer health check** — the DNS provider (Route 53) pings the regional load balancer's IP; if it fails, the DNS stops returning that region's IP. This catches regional-network failures (entire region unreachable). (2) **Regional load balancer health check** — the regional LB (ALB) pings its backend instances; if instances fail, the LB removes them and returns 503 if no backends are healthy. This catches backend-instance failures. (3) **Origin/dependency health check** — the backend pings its database, cache, and downstream services; if the DB is unreachable, the backend returns 503 even though it's "alive." This catches cascading-dependency failures (the backend process is healthy but functionally broken because DB is down). A common failure: DNS health check passes (LB responds to TCP SYN) but every request returns 500 because the DB is down — traffic continues flowing to a broken region until the origin-level 500s cause the LB's passive health check to eject backends, eventually causing the LB to return 503, eventually causing DNS to fail its probe. Layered checks catch failures faster and more precisely.
**Visual:**
```
DNS health check:    can I TCP-connect to region's LB?
LB health check:     do backends respond to /healthz?
Origin health check: can backend reach DB/cache/downstream?

miss any layer -> false-positive "healthy" routing -> client sees 500s
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You operate an e-commerce site in the US and EU. A user in Japan reports the site is slow. How do you diagnose and fix it with global load balancing?
**Answer:** First, confirm the user is being routed to the wrong region. Check the DNS resolver they're using — if it's a Japanese resolver that supports EDNS Client Subnet, the authoritative DNS should return an APAC-region IP if one exists, or the lowest-latency of US/EU. If ECS isn't supported and the resolver is in the US (e.g., 8.8.8.1 sometimes routes through US infrastructure), the user may be hitting the US region (180ms RTT) instead of EU (250ms — actually slower). Diagnose with `dig +trace api.example.com` from the user's network, and check the authoritative DNS's logs for which region IP was returned for their /24. The fix depends on findings: (a) if no APAC region exists, add one and update DNS to route Japanese /24s there; (b) if APAC exists but the user's resolver doesn't support ECS, consider a Cloudflare Worker or geo-redirect at the edge that re-homes them; (c) if the user's resolver is misbehaving, recommend they switch resolvers. Long-term, deploy anycast-based DNS (so the resolver itself reaches a nearby authoritative nameserver) and consider edge compute (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge) to terminate the request close to the user regardless of region routing.
**Visual:**
```
Japan user --DNS--> 8.8.8.8 (US resolver, no ECS) --> returns US IP
                                                          (180ms slow)
fix: add APAC region + ECS-aware DNS OR edge compute
```

### Q2. Your multi-region active-active service has a 60-second DNS TTL. A region fails at 14:00. At 14:05, you still see 5% of traffic hitting the failed region. Why?
**Answer:** Three common causes. (1) **Long-lived connections** — HTTP/2, WebSocket, and gRPC connections established before the failure persist up to the connection's keep-alive timeout (often 5-10 minutes for HTTP/2). DNS TTL only affects new connections, not existing ones. The fix is aggressive server-side connection draining, but clients with stale connections will still hit the dead region until they reconnect. (2) **Stubborn DNS caches** — some clients (older Androids, embedded devices, certain OS DNS resolvers) ignore short TTLs and cache for longer (sometimes hours). The 60-second TTL is a hint, not a command. (3) **Application-level DNS caching** — many HTTP clients and SDKs cache DNS results in-process (Java's default JVM DNS cache is 30 seconds, but some apps configure 5+ minutes). The fix: set `networkaddress.cache.ttl=60` in JVM, ensure HTTP client connection pools refresh DNS periodically. Operationally, you should expect that ~5-10% of traffic will continue hitting a failed region for several minutes after a regional failure, and your failover story must account for that — typically by having the failed region's load balancer return HTTP 503 with `Retry-After` so clients retry to a different region's IP (which they'll get on the next DNS lookup).
**Visual:**
```
14:00 region fails
14:00-14:01 DNS stops returning failed-region IP (TTL=60s)
14:01-14:05 5% traffic still hits failed region:
   - HTTP/2 keep-alive (5-10 min)
   - JVM DNS cache (60s, but some apps override)
   - stubborn OS caches
```

### Q3. You're designing a global SaaS with users in 50 countries. Should you use DNS-based routing or anycast?
**Answer:** Depends on the workload. **Anycast** is better if (a) the protocol is short-lived or connectionless (DNS, NTP, HTTP/3 over QUIC, CDN static assets), (b) you operate a global edge network or use a CDN (Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai), (c) you need DDoS dilution as a side benefit, and (d) you can re-origin from the edge to the origin via unicast. **DNS-based routing** is better if (a) you have long-lived TCP connections (gRPC streams, WebSocket), (b) you operate in a few cloud regions (not a global edge network), (c) you need fine-grained policies (weighted, geolocation country-level, latency-aware), and (d) you want to fail over between regions on health. For a SaaS with users in 50 countries and a few cloud regions (say 3-5 regions), the answer is almost always DNS-based with a managed DNS provider (Route 53, Cloudflare DNS). Anycast at the application layer requires operating your own BGP announcements or using a CDN — typically you'd put a CDN/anycast layer in front for static assets and DDoS protection, and DNS-based routing for dynamic API calls to your origin regions. Real-world: Netflix uses Route 53 latency-based routing for their API and Cloudflare/anycast CDN for static assets.
**Visual:**
```
anycast: edge network (Cloudflare, Fastly) -> for static + DDoS
DNS-LB:  few cloud regions -> for dynamic API + active-active failover
hybrid:  CDN anycast edge -> DNS-LB origin regions
```

### Q4. During a regional AWS outage, your global LB fails over to a backup region, but the backup region's latency spikes from 50ms to 800ms for users. What happened and how do you prevent it?
**Answer:** The backup region is now absorbing the full traffic of the failed region (potentially 2x its normal load), causing backend saturation, queue buildup, and latency explosion. Two compounding issues. (1) **No pre-warmed capacity in the backup** — if the backup was running at minimum capacity for active-passive, it needs to scale up to handle the failed region's load, and autoscaling takes minutes. (2) **No traffic-shaping on failover** — all of the failed region's traffic shifts at once, overwhelming the backup before autoscaling responds. Prevention: (a) run active-active so all regions are already at full capacity and a failover only adds the failed region's load to regions already handling their share (each region's load goes from 100% to ~150%, not from 10% to 200%); (b) pre-warm the backup region's capacity (keep it at 50% of peak, scale on failover signal); (c) implement rate-limiting / traffic-shaping at the global LB during failover (reject a fraction of traffic rather than overload the backup); (d) use circuit breakers on the client side so they retry with backoff instead of hammering the backup. Operationally, drill failover regularly (GameDays, like Netflix's Simian Army Chaos Monkey + regional failover tests) to validate capacity assumptions.
**Visual:**
```
normal:        EU 50% / US 50%           (active-active)
EU fails:      EU 0% / US 100%           (US overloads, 800ms)
fix: US at 100%, autoscale + rate-limit + active-active from start
```

### Q5. You use Route 53 latency-based routing. A user in India reports being routed to the US region (200ms) instead of the APAC region (40ms). How do you debug?
**Answer:** First, check whether the user's resolver supports EDNS Client Subnet (ECS). If they're using a resolver that doesn't support ECS (e.g., Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 from a privacy mode, or a corporate resolver), Route 53 sees the resolver's IP, not the user's. If the resolver is in the US (some corporate VPNs route DNS through US), Route 53 will return the US region as lowest-latency to the resolver. Debug with `dig +subnet=203.0.113.0/32 api.example.com @1.1.1.1` (manually specifying ECS) and see if the response changes — if so, ECS is the issue. Second, check Route 53's latency database — it's based on AWS's global probing network, which may have sparse coverage for some Indian /24 prefixes, leading to a default-to-US fallback. Third, check whether the APAC region's health check is failing — Route 53 may have excluded APAC from the response because its health check failed, even though the region is technically up (false negative). Solutions: (a) switch the user to a resolver that supports ECS (Google 8.8.8.8 supports ECS in most regions); (b) use geolocation routing as a fallback for India (always route Indian GeoIP to APAC); (c) investigate Route 53's health check configuration for APAC.
**Visual:**
```
India user -> resolver (no ECS, in US) -> Route 53 sees US IP
                                       -> returns US region (200ms)
debug: dig +subnet=... @1.1.1.1 -> reveals ECS issue
fix:   use geolocation routing for India as a fallback
```

### Q6. Your global service uses DynamoDB Global Tables with eventual consistency. A user in EU updates their profile, then immediately (within 200ms) a US-region request reads the profile. The user sees stale data. How do you handle this?
**Answer:** This is the classic "read-after-write consistency across regions" problem with eventual-consistency replication. DynamoDB Global Tables propagate writes within ~1 second typically, but during that window, reads in other regions return stale data. Three approaches. (1) **Accept it for non-critical fields** — most profile fields (avatar, bio) are fine if stale for 1 second; the user rarely reads their own profile from another region in that window. (2) **Sticky reads after writes** — for 5-30 seconds after a user writes, route their reads to the region that handled the write (the "write region"), bypassing global LB. This requires the client or LB to track "last write region" per user (often via a cookie or session token). (3) **Strongly-consistent store for critical fields** — for fields that must be consistent (e.g., account-deletion flag, security settings), use Spanner or CockroachDB with synchronous cross-region replication, accepting the write-latency cost. The production pattern is tiered: most data in DynamoDB Global Tables (eventual), critical flags in a strongly-consistent store, and application-level "read-your-writes" via session affinity for the brief window after a write. Always document the consistency model for users — "your changes may take up to 1 second to appear in other regions" is honest and usually acceptable.
**Visual:**
```
EU user writes profile -> DynamoDB EU (immediate)
                         -> propagates to US (in ~1s)
                         -> US user reads in 200ms -> STALE

fix: sticky reads after write (30s window) -> route reads to EU
     OR strongly-consistent store for critical fields
```

### Q7. Your DNS provider has an outage. Even though your origin servers are healthy, users can't reach your service. How do you protect against this?
**Answer:** DNS is a single point of failure for any Internet-facing service — if no one can resolve your domain, your origin might as well be down. Protection requires redundancy at the DNS layer itself. (1) **Use multiple DNS providers** — configure your domain's NS records at the registrar to point to two or more DNS providers (Route 53 + Cloudflare DNS, or Route 53 + NS1). If one provider fails, the recursive resolver falls back to the next NS record. (2) **Use anycast DNS** — both Route 53 and Cloudflare announce their nameserver IPs via anycast from dozens of PoPs, so a regional network failure doesn't take down the entire DNS provider; but a provider-wide software bug still affects all PoPs. (3) **Set long TTLs at the registrar for NS records** (24+ hours) so a DNS-provider outage doesn't immediately cascade to resolver-level NS re-queries. (4) **Have a backup plan** — keep a static IP for your service that you can publish via social media/status page if DNS is fully down, or pre-distribute an emergency IP via a mobile app's hardcoded fallback. Real-world: in the 2021 Fastly outage, many sites that depended on Fastly for both CDN and DNS were unreachable for ~1 hour; the lesson is to not have DNS and CDN from the same provider, or to have a secondary DNS path. The cost of multi-provider DNS is small ($50-200/month per provider) and the benefit is enormous.
**Visual:**
```
registrar NS records:
  ns1.example.com -> Route 53 (anycast, 60 PoPs)
  ns2.example.com -> Cloudflare DNS (anycast, 300 PoPs)
  ns3.example.com -> NS1 (anycast, 30 PoPs)

Route 53 down? -> resolvers use Cloudflare via NS fallback
                  (small downtime = NS record TTL, typically minutes)
```
